stages.label: Smooth purees
stages.description: Very smooth, strained or pureed foods, thinned with breast milk, formula or water.

stages.label: Thicker purees and mashed
stages.description: Thicker purees and soft foods mashed with a fork, a little less smooth each week.

stages.label: Lumpy and soft finger foods
stages.description: Mashed and lumpy textures, plus soft finger foods your baby can pick up.

stages.label: Finely chopped
stages.description: Finely chopped or ground foods and a wide range of soft finger foods.

stages.label: Chopped family foods
stages.description: Soft, chopped versions of family meals, cut into pieces no bigger than about 1/2 inch.

weeks.title: First tastes
focus: [PLACEHOLDER - needs expert review] Start small: half a spoonful to a teaspoon or two of a single smooth puree, once a day, at a calm time. Some parents give a little breast milk or formula first.
Breast milk or formula is still your baby's main nutrition. This week is about getting used to the spoon and new tastes.
tryFoods: Iron-fortified oat or barley infant cereal
tips: Offer foods rich in iron and zinc, like pureed meat or iron-fortified cereal.
Mix cereal with breast milk, formula or water; never put cereal in a bottle.

weeks.title: More first foods
focus: [PLACEHOLDER - needs expert review] Keep offering one new single-ingredient food at a time, building up toward 1 to 2 tablespoons as your baby is ready.
Watch for fullness cues: closing the mouth or turning away means they've had enough.
tips: Vary infant cereals (oat, barley, multigrain) rather than only rice cereal.
Freeze small portions of purees in ice-cube trays to save time.

weeks.title: First allergen
focus: [PLACEHOLDER - needs expert review] Once your baby has had a few first foods without problems, you can start offering common allergens, one at a time, alongside other foods.
If your baby has severe, persistent eczema or has reacted to a food before, talk to your pediatrician first.

allergen.label: Egg
allergen.howTo: A small taste of well-cooked egg, mashed or thinned (hard-boiled or scrambled until fully set).

tips: Introduce one new food at a time so you can spot any reaction.
Once a food is tolerated, keep offering it regularly.

allergen.label: Peanut
allergen.howTo: A small amount of smooth peanut butter thinned into cereal, fruit puree or yogurt, or dissolved in breast milk or formula. Never whole peanuts.

tips: Introduce one new food at a time so you can spot any reaction.
Once a food is tolerated, keep offering it regularly.

readiness.intro: [PLACEHOLDER - needs expert review] Most babies are ready for solid foods at about 6 months. Starting before 4 months isn't recommended. Look for these signs together:
signs: Sits up alone or with support
Opens their mouth when food comes their way
Swallows food rather than pushing it out onto their chin
Tries to grasp small objects, like toys or food

choking.intro: [PLACEHOLDER - needs expert review] Choking is silent and serious. Gagging (coughing, sputtering, pushing food forward) is a normal part of learning to eat. Know the difference, and consider an infant CPR and first-aid class.
signs: Can't breathe, cry or make a sound

groups.title: At every meal
items: Always watch your child while they eat.
Sit them upright in a high chair or safe seat; no eating while lying down, crawling, walking, or in the car or stroller.
Serve foods with the right texture for their stage.

groups.title: 6 to 12 months: avoid or change
items: Whole or chopped nuts and seeds; chunks or spoonfuls of nut butter (thin it instead).
Whole grapes, cherries, berries, cherry tomatoes and melon balls (cut into small pieces).
Raw hard vegetables or fruit like carrots and apples (cook until soft).
Hot dogs, sausages and meat sticks; tough or large chunks of meat; bones in meat or fish.
Chunks of cheese, especially string cheese (cut into short, thin strips).
Whole corn kernels, whole beans, raisins and other dried fruit.
Popcorn, chips, pretzels, crackers or bread with seeds or whole grains, granola bars.
Hard, round or sticky candy, gummies, marshmallows and gum.

groups.title: 1 to 4 years: still take care
items: Children don't chew with a grinding motion until about age 4.
Cut food into pieces no larger than about 1/2 inch.
Quarter grapes and cherry tomatoes; cut hot dogs lengthwise, then into small pieces.
Spread nut butter thinly on bread or a cracker; never by the spoonful.
Keep high-risk foods like whole nuts, popcorn and hard candy away until about age 4 or later.
